text: This information is for adults aged 18 or over. There's separate information about paracetamol for children (Calpol).

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: How you take or use paracetamol depends on the type you're taking and other factors. For example, if you weigh less than 50kg, you may need to take a lower dose. Always check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: For 500mg tablets and capsules: one dose is 1 or 2 tablets or capsules; leave at least 4 hours between each dose; do not take more than 8 tablets or capsules in 24 hours.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: You can sometimes get 1g (1000mg) tablets either on prescription or from a pharmacy. If you're taking these, you should only take one at a time and do not take more than 4 tablets in 24 hours.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: For 250mg/5ml oral suspension: one dose is 10ml to 20ml; leave at least 4 hours between doses; do not take it more than 4 doses in 24 hours.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: For 500mg/5ml oral suspension: one dose is 5ml to 10ml; leave at least 4 hours between doses; do not take it more than 4 times in 24 hours.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: Do not take or use paracetamol for more than 3 days unless a doctor tells you to. You should also avoid taking paracetamol at the same time as other medicines containing paracetamol, for example, cold and flu remedies. This is because you may take too much, which can be dangerous.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: Taking an extra dose of paracetamol is unlikely to cause problems, but it's important to get medical advice if you take too much as it can sometimes damage your liver. Get help from NHS 111 if you've taken more paracetamol than it says on the packet or leaflet.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening allergic reaction that happens very quickly. It can be caused by food, medicine or insect stings. Call 999 if you think you or someone else is having an anaphylactic reaction.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: Use an adrenaline auto-injector (such as an EpiPen) if you have one. Call 999 for an ambulance and say that you think you're having an anaphylactic reaction. Lie down; you can raise your legs, and if you're struggling to breathe, raise your shoulders or sit up slowly (if you're pregnant, lie on your left side).

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: If your symptoms have not improved after 5 minutes, use a 2nd adrenaline auto-injector.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: Common symptoms of sepsis in adults include: confusion or slurred speech; uncontrollable shivering; muscle pain; difficulty breathing; blue, pale, grey or blotchy skin, lips or tongue; a high or low temperature; not peeing all day or peeing very little in the past 18 hours.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: Call 999 or go to A&E if a baby or child under 5 years has a very high temperature: 38C or more in babies under 3 months old, or 39C or more in babies 3 to 6 months old; or a very low temperature: less than 36C, or feels cold to the touch or is shivery.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: Sepsis is treated in hospital. Treatment depends on things like your age and how unwell you are. Treatment for sepsis includes: antibiotics (you may be given a general antibiotic to start with and then a more specific one after the cause of the infection has been confirmed); oxygen to help with breathing; fluids given into a vein to help rehydrate you.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: If a doctor thinks you have DVT (deep vein thrombosis), you should be referred to hospital within 24 hours for an ultrasound scan.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: You'll usually need to take blood-thinning medicines, such as rivaroxaban, for at least 3 months to reduce your risk of getting another blood clot. These medicines are usually taken as tablets.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: If you get a DVT when you're pregnant, you'll usually need blood-thinning injections for the rest of your pregnancy and until your baby is 6 weeks old.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: Delay any flights or long journeys until at least 2 weeks after you start taking blood-thinning medicine.

licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, NHS website content
text: Call 999 or go to A&E if an adult or child aged 5 years or over: is breathing very fast; is confused, has slurred speech, or is not making sense; has blue, pale or blotchy skin; has a very high or very low temperature, feels hot or cold to the touch, or is shivery; has a rash that does not fade when you press it; has symptoms you're worried might be sepsis.
